The applicant \nshould provide a plan for maintaining configuration throughout the product life cycle. \nIf the installation results in a modification to the laser equipment as certified by the However, most airborne surveillance lasers and some LIDARs exceed the \nallowable class I AELs for the invisible wavelengths and therefore require variances as \ndescribed in § 1010.4. For products labeled under the classification system of the IEC, \nclasses 1, 2, and 3R are acceptable class limits for an invisible emission and therefore \ndo not require a variance. The FDA variance may require administrative controls \n(for example, the laser equipment purchasing organization is to maintain an active \nprogram of training for its employees in the safe use of the laser system) and technical \ncontrols (such as a range finder cutoff that disables the laser when the distance between \nthe laser’s aperture and the object being exposed is less than the NOHD).\n7.3 Aircraft Laser Equipment Installation.\n7.3.1 System Safety Analysis.\nYou must perform a system safety analysis to assess whether the installed laser \nequipment meets 14 CFR 23.1309, 25.1309, 27.1309, or 29.1309. Refer to \nAC 23.1309-1, System Safety Analysis and Assessment for Part 23 Airplanes. For \npart 25 airplanes, refer to AC 25.1309-1, System Design and Analysis. For part 27 \nrotorcraft, refer to AC 27.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. For part 29\n\nrotorcraft, refer to AC 29.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. The systems \nsafety assessment should address the following:\n7.3.1.1 Laser Equipment Malfunction.\nLaser equipment malfunction resulting in an aircraft crewmember’s or \npassenger’s eye or skin being exposed to invisible laser radiation \nexceeding the MPE is considered no less than a hazardous functional \nfailure condition and could be catastrophic if continued safe flight is not \npossible because of the severity of the laser damage to a pilot’s eye or \nskin. In your system safety assessment, you should document the rationale \nfor a hazardous functional failure condition classification. If there is no \ndirect or reflected path into the cockpit or cabin because of the location of \nthe laser and physical shielding provided by the aircraft structure, this \nfailure condition does not apply. \n7.3.1.2 System Safety Considerations.\nIn assessing the failure conditions, you should consider direct and \nreflected radiation; the location of the laser, laser beam steering \nmechanism, and circuitry; the use of mechanical, software, or airborne \nelectronic hardware (AEH) stops that prevent the laser from being steered \nin a direction that could result in the aircraft occupants’ eyes being \nexposed to direct or reflected radiation; laser arming and firing circuitry; \nand other design features whose malfunction could contribute to an \ninadvertent exposure or an exposure that exceeds the MPE (such as failure \nof the internal laser diffuser used to reduce the AEL). If the laser’s\nsteering stops are implemented in software or AEH, their assurance level \nshould be commensurate with the functional failure condition associated \nwith the stops. Reflections off any part of the aircraft (such as the \nstructure, blades, skids, or landing gear) should be considered specular.\n7.3.1.3 Aircraft Structure. \nAny malfunction resulting in damage to aircraft structure due to laser \nexposure should be assessed to determine the extent of aircraft damage \nand the associated functional failure condition classification.\n7.3.1.4 Equipment Interfaces.\nAny malfunction of the laser equipment’s interfaces with other aircraft \nsystem will have to be assessed to determine the effect on the aircraft \nsystem and laser equipment as well as the associated functional failure \ncondition classifications.","knowledge_id":"813acfd3-492b-45fb-8705-d46a0ccbf984","chunk_index":43,"knowledge_title":"AC_20-183.pdf","start_at":10651,"end_at":11003,"seq":43,"score":0.9286160714285713,"match_type":0,"sub_chunk_id":null,"metadata":{"process_overrides":"map[asr_config:map[enabled:false language: model_id:] chunking_config:map[child_chunk_size:384 chunk_overlap:80 chunk_size:512 enable_parent_child:true parent_chunk_size:4096 separators:[\n\n \n 。 ！ ？ ; during taxi, takeoff, or landing. \n7.3.7.1.3 Laser must not be used to radiate \npeople when the distance between the \nlaser and the people is less than NOHD. \nThe NOHD should be specified. This AC is not mandatory and does not \nconstitute a regulation. This AC describes an acceptable means, but not the only means, \nto comply with the requirements found in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations \n(14 CFR) 23.1301, 23.1309, 23.1529, 23.1581, 25.1301, 25.1309, 25.1529, 25.1581, \n27.1301, 27.1309, 27.1529, 27.1581, 29.1301, 29.1309, 29.1529, and 29.1581 for the \nlaser equipment aspects only. If you use the means described in this AC, you must \nfollow it in its entirety.\n1.2 This AC only addresses unique laser airworthiness installation requirements. It is not \ncomprehensive installation guidance for airborne equipment with lasers because it does \nnot address all the applicable installation airworthiness requirements such as those \ndiscussed in paragraph 7 below. \n1.3 This AC is not intended for installations seeking airworthiness approval of required \naircraft equipment that has a laser with radiation contained within a protective housing \n(for example, a ring laser gyro). \n1.4 This AC is not intended for laser-based weapons and aircraft self-protection \ncountermeasures equipment installations. \n1.5 This AC is only intended for invisible lasers. This AC does not apply to visible lasers \nbecause they pose additional hazards (such as flash blindness) that are not addressed \nin this AC. \n1.6 Additional airworthiness certification criteria beyond what is described in this AC \nwould be required for installations intended for laser operation with head- or \nhelmet-mounted vision devices such as night vision goggles (NVG). For NVG\n\n1.7 guidance, refer to AC 27.1, Certification of Normal Category Rotorcraft, miscellaneous \nguidance (MG) 16, or AC 29.2, Certification of Transport Category Rotorcraft, MG 16. \n2 AUDIENCE.\nWe wrote this AC for aircraft manufacturers, laser equipment manufacturers, \ninstallation shops, and other applicants seeking FAA airworthiness approval of \ninvisible spectrum laser equipment installations on part 23, 25, 27, and 29 aircraft. \nThe airworthiness approval can occur under a type certificate (TC), supplemental type \ncertificate (STC), amended type certificate (ATC), amended supplemental type \ncertificate (ASTC) or data approval for major alteration. This AC also provides \nguidance to FAA personnel involved in a TC, STC, ATC, ASTC, or data approval for \nmajor alterations that install invisible spectrum laser equipment.\n3 BACKGROUND.\n3.1 Laser Surveillance Equipment.\nLocal, State, and Federal law enforcement agencies use forward looking infrared \n(FLIR) equipment with laser illuminators, pointers, and range finders for nighttime, \ncovert surveillance. Laser surveillance equipment may be used to support several kinds \nof tasks and missions, varying from target range-finding to illuminating small spots or \nlarge areas. Certification of such airborne surveillance equipment installations with \nlasers presents some unique challenges because lasers can pose a potential eye hazard\nto flight crew, passengers, other aircraft occupants, and the nonflying public. Laser \nsurveillance equipment typically uses class IIIb or IV lasers. Before this guidance, many \nsurveillance systems were installed using an STC for laser surveillance equipment that \nonly included provisional wiring for the laser. For these installations, the STC type \ndesign would show that the laser was electrically disabled. These installations may have \nnot completely addressed all the laser hazards.","knowledge_id":"813acfd3-492b-45fb-8705-d46a0ccbf984","chunk_index":10,"knowledge_title":"AC_20-183.pdf","start_at":2427,"end_at":2760,"seq":10,"score":0.7615211810012836,"match_type":0,"sub_chunk_id":null,"metadata":{"process_overrides":"map[asr_config:map[enabled:false language: model_id:] chunking_config:map[child_chunk_size:384 chunk_overlap:80 chunk_size:512 enable_parent_child:true parent_chunk_size:4096 separators:[\n\n \n 。 ！ ？ ; ；] strategy:auto] enable_multimodel:false extract_config:map[enabled:false] graph_enabled:false image_actions:map[ocr:map[on:[map[is:block prop:contain.text] map[is:true prop:contain.data_visual]] on_unobserved:true]] image_attrs_enabled:false image_vector_enabled:false question_generation_config:map[enabled:true question_count:3] summary_enabled:true vlm_config:map[api_key: base_url: enabled:false interface_type: model_id: model_name:]]"},"chunk_type":"text","parent_chunk_id":"180d3834-332a-443d-9830-e7f70b9b93e5","image_info":"","knowledge_filename":"AC_20-183.pdf","knowledge_source":"","knowledge_channel":"web","matched_content":"AC_20-183.pdf\n在23、25、27和29部飞机上安装不可见光谱激光设备时，","knowledge_description":"该咨询通告（AC 20-183）为在23、25、27和29部飞机上安装机载、非必需、不可见光谱激光设备（如红外监视激光和LIDAR）提供一种获取FAA适航批准的建议方法。文件明确其非强制性，仅针对激光设备相关的适航要求，并讨论激光监视设备、LIDAR、眼部危害、STC限制、FDA豁免及公共用途等事项。其结论是申请人可完整遵循本AC所述方法，以获得不可见激光设备安装的适航批准。","knowledge_base_id":"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e","source_locators":[{"type":"pdf","mapping":"exact","source_id":"pdf:2:190:829","source_hash":"775a1f9a4fb0e18402f45b394356aa5d","page":2,"bbox":[0.1882,0.1757,0.869,0.3175],"quote":"invisible spectrum laser equipment installations on part 23, 25, 27, and 29 aircraft. These installations may have \nnot completely addressed all the laser hazards.\n3.2 LIDAR.\nA LIDAR uses a laser to perform ranging by measuring the reflected return of a \nprojected laser beam. LIDAR devices can be used in mapping terrain elevation, \nobstacles, and vegetation; or atmospheric measuring (for example, particulate tracking \nor turbulence monitoring). Some LIDARs use an internal class IIIb or IV laser, and \nthrough an internal mechanism, diffuse the external laser emissions to a class I level.\nLIDAR external laser emissions can range from class I to class IV.\n3.3 Eye Hazard.\nFLIR and LIDAR lasers can be especially hazardous because the beam is invisible and\nthere is no blink reflex reaction to protect the eye, so eye exposure may initially go \nundetected. Exposure to lasers operating within the 750 to 1,400 nanometer (nm) \nnear infrared spectrum can cause retinal eye damage. The 400 to 1,400 nm wave band is \nknown as the retinal hazard region. Laser equipment that operates in the 315 to 400 nm \nultraviolet or the 1,400 to 10,600 nm far infrared spectrums can damage the cornea,\n\nlens, or both. Most FLIR and LIDAR lasers operate with a wavelength of 800 to \n1570 nm. The extent of eye damage depends on the laser exposure dose.\n4 ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES.\n4.1 FAA Regulatory Authority Role. \nThe FAA is responsible for issuing a design approval (such as an STC) or other data \napproval for an aircraft laser installation when an applicant demonstrates the laser \ninstallation meets the applicable airworthiness requirements.\n4.2 Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Regulatory Authority Role.\nThe FDA has the authority to regulate light-emitting products and electronic product \nradiation (Title 21 of the United States Code section 360ii, Program of control). The \nFDA is also responsible for approval or disapproval of variance applications for a laser \nnot meeting the laser performance standards found in Title 21 of the Code Federal \nRegulations (21 CFR) part 1040, Performance Standards for Light-Emitting Products.\n4.3 Laser Manufacturer Equipment Certification Role.\nThe laser manufacturer is responsible for self-certifying that the laser meets the \nperformance standards in § 1040.10, Laser products, and obtaining a variance \nfrom the FDA when laser equipment does not meet a laser performance standard.\n4.4 Installation Applicant Role.\nThe applicant who applies for an installation design approval is responsible for \nmeeting all applicable FAA airworthiness and FDA laser performance and \nvariance requirements.\n5 DEFINITIONS.\n5.1 Accessible Emission Limit (AEL).\nThe maximum accessible emission level permitted by the FDA within a particular \nlaser hazard class as stated in § 1040.10(c), (d), and (e).\n5.2 Divergence.\nThe increase in diameter of the laser beam with distance from the exit aperture. \nDivergence is an angular measurement of the beam spread, expressed in milliradians \n(mrad) defined at the points where the irradiance is 37 percent of the peak irradiance. \n5.3 Irradiance.\nA means of expressing power of the beam per unit area, which is expressed in \nwatts per centimeter squared (W/cm2).\n\n5.4 Maximum Permissible Exposure (MPE). \nThe level of laser radiation to which an unprotected person may be exposed without \nhazardous effect or adverse biological change in the eye or skin, normally expressed \nin milliwatts per centimeter squared (mW/cm2) or millijoules per centimeter \nsquared (mJ/cm2).\n5.5 Nominal Ocular Hazard Distance (NOHD). \nThe distance from the laser beyond which the laser radiation does not exceed the However, most airborne surveillance lasers and some LIDARs exceed the \nallowable class I AELs for the invisible wavelengths and therefore require variances as \ndescribed in § 1010.4. For products labeled under the classification system of the IEC, \nclasses 1, 2, and 3R are acceptable class limits for an invisible emission and therefore \ndo not require a variance. The FDA variance may require administrative controls \n(for example, the laser equipment purchasing organization is to maintain an active \nprogram of training for its employees in the safe use of the laser system) and technical \ncontrols (such as a range finder cutoff that disables the laser when the distance between \nthe laser’s aperture and the object being exposed is less than the NOHD).\n7.3 Aircraft Laser Equipment Installation.\n7.3.1 System Safety Analysis.\nYou must perform a system safety analysis to assess whether the installed laser \nequipment meets 14 CFR 23.1309, 25.1309, 27.1309, or 29.1309. Refer to \nAC 23.1309-1, System Safety Analysis and Assessment for Part 23 Airplanes. For \npart 25 airplanes, refer to AC 25.1309-1, System Design and Analysis. For part 27 \nrotorcraft, refer to AC 27.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. For part 29\n\nrotorcraft, refer to AC 29.1309, Equipment, Systems and Installations. The systems \nsafety assessment should address the following:\n7.3.1.1 Laser Equipment Malfunction.\nLaser equipment malfunction resulting in an aircraft crewmember’s or \npassenger’s eye or skin being exposed to invisible laser radiation \nexceeding the MPE is considered no less than a hazardous functional \nfailure condition and could be catastrophic if continued safe flight is not \npossible because of the severity of the laser damage to a pilot’s eye or \nskin. In your system safety assessment, you should document the rationale \nfor a hazardous functional failure condition classification. If there is no \ndirect or reflected path into the cockpit or cabin because of the location of \nthe laser and physical shielding provided by the aircraft structure, this \nfailure condition does not apply. \n7.3.1.2 System Safety Considerations.\nIn assessing the failure conditions, you should consider direct and \nreflected radiation; the location of the laser, laser beam steering \nmechanism, and circuitry; the use of mechanical, software, or airborne \nelectronic hardware (AEH) stops that prevent the laser from being steered \nin a direction that could result in the aircraft occupants’ eyes being \nexposed to direct or reflected radiation; laser arming and firing circuitry; \nand other design features whose malfunction could contribute to an \ninadvertent exposure or an exposure that exceeds the MPE (such as failure \nof the internal laser diffuser used to reduce the AEL). If the laser’s\nsteering stops are implemented in software or AEH, their assurance level \nshould be commensurate with the functional failure condition associated \nwith the stops. Reflections off any part of the aircraft (such as the \nstructure, blades, skids, or landing gear) should be considered specular.\n7.3.1.3 Aircraft Structure. \nAny malfunction resulting in damage to aircraft structure due to laser \nexposure should be assessed to determine the extent of aircraft damage \nand the associated functional failure condition classification.\n7.3.1.4 Equipment Interfaces.\nAny malfunction of the laser equipment’s interfaces with other aircraft \nsystem will have to be assessed to determine the effect on the aircraft \nsystem and laser equipment as well as the associated functional failure \ncondition classifications.","end_at":11003,"id":"91357a97-ff8d-402d-be66-b2003ba885ab","image_info":"","knowledge_base_id":"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e","knowledge_channel":"web","knowledge_description":"该咨询通告（AC 20-183）为在23、25、27和29部飞机上安装机载、非必需、不可见光谱激光设备（如红外监视激光和LIDAR）提供一种获取FAA适航批准的建议方法。文件明确其非强制性，仅针对激光设备相关的适航要求，并讨论激光监视设备、LIDAR、眼部危害、STC限制、FDA豁免及公共用途等事项。其结论是申请人可完整遵循本AC所述方法，以获得不可见激光设备安装的适航批准。","knowledge_filename":"AC_20-183.pdf","knowledge_id":"813acfd3-492b-45fb-8705-d46a0ccbf984","knowledge_source":"","knowledge_title":"AC_20-183.pdf","match_type":0,"matched_content":"AC_20-183.pdf\n根据§1040.11(b)，监视、水准和准直激光产品在不可见波长下的AEL限制是什么？","metadata":{"process_overrides":"map[asr_config:map[enabled:false language: model_id:] chunking_config:map[child_chunk_size:384 chunk_overlap:80 chunk_size:512 enable_parent_child:true parent_chunk_size:4096 separators:[\n\n \n 。 ！ ？ ; This AC is not mandatory and does not \nconstitute a regulation. This AC describes an acceptable means, but not the only means, \nto comply with the requirements found in Title 14 of the Code of Federal Regulations \n(14 CFR) 23.1301, 23.1309, 23.1529, 23.1581, 25.1301, 25.1309, 25.1529, 25.1581, \n27.1301, 27.1309, 27.1529, 27.1581, 29.1301, 29.1309, 29.1529, and 29.1581 for the \nlaser equipment aspects only. If you use the means described in this AC, you must \nfollow it in its entirety.\n1.2 This AC only addresses unique laser airworthiness installation requirements. It is not \ncomprehensive installation guidance for airborne equipment with lasers because it does \nnot address all the applicable installation airworthiness requirements such as those \ndiscussed in paragraph 7 below. \n1.3 This AC is not intended for installations seeking airworthiness approval of required \naircraft equipment that has a laser with radiation contained within a protective housing \n(for example, a ring laser gyro). \n1.4 This AC is not intended for laser-based weapons and aircraft self-protection \ncountermeasures equipment installations. \n1.5 This AC is only intended for invisible lasers. This AC does not apply to visible lasers \nbecause they pose additional hazards (such as flash blindness) that are not addressed \nin this AC. \n1.6 Additional airworthiness certification criteria beyond what is described in this AC \nwould be required for installations intended for laser operation with head- or \nhelmet-mounted vision devices such as night vision goggles (NVG). For NVG\n\n1.7 guidance, refer to AC 27.1, Certification of Normal Category Rotorcraft, miscellaneous \nguidance (MG) 16, or AC 29.2, Certification of Transport Category Rotorcraft, MG 16. \n2 AUDIENCE.\nWe wrote this AC for aircraft manufacturers, laser equipment manufacturers, \ninstallation shops, and other applicants seeking FAA airworthiness approval of \ninvisible spectrum laser equipment installations on part 23, 25, 27, and 29 aircraft. \nThe airworthiness approval can occur under a type certificate (TC), supplemental type \ncertificate (STC), amended type certificate (ATC), amended supplemental type \ncertificate (ASTC) or data approval for major alteration. This AC also provides \nguidance to FAA personnel involved in a TC, STC, ATC, ASTC, or data approval for \nmajor alterations that install invisible spectrum laser equipment.\n3 BACKGROUND.\n3.1 Laser Surveillance Equipment.\nLocal, State, and Federal law enforcement agencies use forward looking infrared \n(FLIR) equipment with laser illuminators, pointers, and range finders for nighttime, \ncovert surveillance. Laser surveillance equipment may be used to support several kinds \nof tasks and missions, varying from target range-finding to illuminating small spots or \nlarge areas. Certification of such airborne surveillance equipment installations with \nlasers presents some unique challenges because lasers can pose a potential eye hazard\nto flight crew, passengers, other aircraft occupants, and the nonflying public. Laser \nsurveillance equipment typically uses class IIIb or IV lasers. Before this guidance, many \nsurveillance systems were installed using an STC for laser surveillance equipment that \nonly included provisional wiring for the laser. For these installations, the STC type \ndesign would show that the laser was electrically disabled. These installations may have \nnot completely addressed all the laser hazards.\n3.2 LIDAR.\nA LIDAR uses a laser to perform ranging by measuring the reflected return of a \nprojected laser beam. LIDAR devices can be used in mapping terrain elevation, \nobstacles, and vegetation; or atmospheric measuring (for example, particulate tracking \nor turbulence monitoring). Some LIDARs use an internal class IIIb or IV laser, and \nthrough an internal mechanism, diffuse the external laser emissions to a class I level.\nLIDAR external laser emissions can range from class I to class IV.\n3.3 Eye Hazard.\nFLIR and LIDAR lasers can be especially hazardous because the beam is invisible and\nthere is no blink reflex reaction to protect the eye, so eye exposure may initially go \nundetected. Exposure to lasers operating within the 750 to 1,400 nanometer (nm) \nnear infrared spectrum can cause retinal eye damage. The 400 to 1,400 nm wave band is \nknown as the retinal hazard region. Laser equipment that operates in the 315 to 400 nm \nultraviolet or the 1,400 to 10,600 nm far infrared spectrums can damage the cornea,\n\nlens, or both. Most FLIR and LIDAR lasers operate with a wavelength of 800 to \n1570 nm. The extent of eye damage depends on the laser exposure dose.\n4 ROLES AND RESPONSIBILITIES.\n4.1 FAA Regulatory Authority Role. \nThe FAA is responsible for issuing a design approval (such as an STC) or other data \napproval for an aircraft laser installation when an applicant demonstrates the laser \ninstallation meets the applicable airworthiness requirements.\n4.2 Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Regulatory Authority Role.\nThe FDA has the authority to regulate light-emitting products and electronic product \nradiation (Title 21 of the United States Code section 360ii, Program of control). The \nFDA is also responsible for approval or disapproval of variance applications for a laser \nnot meeting the laser performance standards found in Title 21 of the Code Federal \nRegulations (21 CFR) part 1040, Performance Standards for Light-Emitting Products.\n4.3 Laser Manufacturer Equipment Certification Role.\nThe laser manufacturer is responsible for self-certifying that the laser meets the \nperformance standards in § 1040.10, Laser products, and obtaining a variance \nfrom the FDA when laser equipment does not meet a laser performance standard.\n4.4 Installation Applicant Role.\nThe applicant who applies for an installation design approval is responsible for \nmeeting all applicable FAA airworthiness and FDA laser performance and \nvariance requirements.\n5 DEFINITIONS.\n5.1 Accessible Emission Limit (AEL).\nThe maximum accessible emission level permitted by the FDA within a particular \nlaser hazard class as stated in § 1040.10(c), (d), and (e).\n5.2 Divergence.\nThe increase in diameter of the laser beam with distance from the exit aperture. \nDivergence is an angular measurement of the beam spread, expressed in milliradians \n(mrad) defined at the points where the irradiance is 37 percent of the peak irradiance. \n5.3 Irradiance.\nA means of expressing power of the beam per unit area, which is expressed in \nwatts per centimeter squared (W/cm2).\n\n5.4 Maximum Permissible Exposure (MPE). \nThe level of laser radiation to which an unprotected person may be exposed without \nhazardous effect or adverse biological change in the eye or skin, normally expressed \nin milliwatts per centimeter squared (mW/cm2) or millijoules per centimeter \nsquared (mJ/cm2).\n5.5 Nominal Ocular Hazard Distance (NOHD). \nThe distance from the laser beyond which the laser radiation does not exceed the data:{"id":"c2f4c177-fbc5-4c27-8c50-3b58f367da08","response_type":"complete","content":"","done":true,"data":{"final_content":"**结论：** 仅凭现有材料，无法给出一个可辩护的精确 NOHD 数值。不过，可以确定一项关键参数：**计算曝光时长应取 10 s，而不是任务最长的 3 s**。\n\n\u003e 说明：本次检索实际只返回了 **AC 20-183** 的内容，未见到其余六份文件；因此下面只依据该 AC 作答，不能假装已经完成了对七份文件的交叉计算。\n\n## 1. 可以确定的计算时长下限\n\nAC 20-183 对不扫描激光明确规定：\n\n\u003e “For laser illuminators, spotters, range finders, and other nonscanning lasers, the NOHD exposure duration should be based on the maximum exposure duration expected, but not less than 10 seconds.”\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"1a2b68d6-e33c-4fda-b226-0e7f612a94ad\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e\n\n因此，即使单次任务预计最长只照射 3 s，NOHD 计算仍应取：\n\n**t_calc = max（预计最大曝光时长, 10 s）= 10 s**\n\n这里的 10 s 是计算假设的下限，并非设备实际会连续照射 10 s。如果实际预期最大曝光时间超过 10 s，就应改用更大的值。10 s 只是“时长下限”，还不是 NOHD 数值。\n\n## 2. 仍算不出精确 NOHD 的原因\n\nNOHD 的定义是：激光辐射不超过 MPE 的距离\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"34453ec1-4c95-44ed-9ef3-de367a101fe3\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e。要算出数值，必须同时知道 MPE 和激光束参数。AC 20-183 将 MPE/NOHD 的计算方法指向 AC 70-1 和 ANSI Z136.1\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"1a2b68d6-e33c-4fda-b226-0e7f612a94ad\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"cd389c51-3c16-487e-b4ad-db68432ab4ed\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e，但本次检索到的内容没有给出 1550 nm、10 s 条件下可直接代入的 MPE 数值或表格。\n\n1550 nm 位于 1,400–10,600 nm 远红外波段，主要危害是角膜和晶状体\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"68e596a2-27ed-4da2-8569-20c930653521\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e，但这仍不能替代具体的 MPE 限值。\n\n此外，AC 明确要求计算报告列出公式、公式来源、表号、波长、发散角、曝光时间、功率，以及直接和反射光路进入飞机窗户的尺寸等参数\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"6fb4573b-f049-4fa1-a093-e61eb66e0b29\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e。目前缺少这些输入，所以无法得出唯一数值。\n\n## 3. 复算所需的一般公式与输入\n\n在工程复算中，圆形均匀光束可写成：\n\n**NOHD = [ √(4P / (π·MPE)) − D ] / θ**\n\n其中：P 为功率（W），MPE 为辐照度限值（W/cm²），D 为出射光束直径（cm），θ 为全角发散角（rad）。若厂家给出的是 mrad，需先换算。该式只是复算框架，**不是 AC 20-183 原文公式**；正式报告还应按 AC 要求注明公式来源和表号\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"6fb4573b-f049-4fa1-a093-e61eb66e0b29\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e。高斯光束还需按峰值辐照度和 1/e² 束径修正，不能直接套用。\n\n要得到精确 NOHD，至少需要补充：\n\n| 所需证据 | 具体内容 |\n|---|---|\n| 激光输出参数 | 1550 nm 确认、平均功率或脉冲能量/重频/脉宽、出射口径、全角发散角、光束轮廓 |\n| MPE 依据 | ANSI Z136.1 的具体版本、表号或公式；1550 nm、10 s、眼部（角膜）限值 |\n| 光路几何 | 直接路径及镜面反射路径到驾驶舱/客舱窗户的距离、入射角、窗口透射率；飞机结构反射应按镜面反射考虑\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"f9de2a39-eeb9-4c30-9f5e-ba96ccfd1cb7\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e |\n| 计算报告 | 公式、公式引用、表号、全部参数、直接/反射光路尺寸及曝光时长合理性说明\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"6fb4573b-f049-4fa1-a093-e61eb66e0b29\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e |\n\n## 4. 目前能给出的确定答案\n\n- **NOHD 精确数值：无法计算**，缺少功率、发散角、束径和 1550 nm/10 s 的 MPE 限值。\n- **计算曝光时长下限：10 s**；不是 3 s。若实际最大曝光时长大于 10 s，则取实际值\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"1a2b68d6-e33c-4fda-b226-0e7f612a94ad\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e。\n- **需要的关键证据：** 激光功率/能量参数、发散角与束径、ANSI Z136.1 的 MPE 表或公式，以及直接和镜面反射光路几何\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"6fb4573b-f049-4fa1-a093-e61eb66e0b29\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e\u003ckb doc=\"AC_20-183.pdf\" chunk_id=\"cd389c51-3c16-487e-b4ad-db68432ab4ed\" kb_id=\"ec1ebcc3-6d50-46d6-8a64-5444dce0962e\" /\u003e。\n\n拿到上述数据后，才能把 P、θ、D 和 MPE 代入公式，给出可复核的 NOHD 数值及适用条件。","total_duration_ms":0,"total_steps":0}}
